brief.head: Weber’s community
brief.text: The state is not a set of in­sti­tu­tions, Ajay Shah said, cit­ing Max Weber, but a com­mu­nity of peo­ple hold­ing a mo­nop­oly of phys­i­cal vi­o­lence over a ter­ri­tory. {033-C02}

brief.head: If Nehru were alive
brief.text: Freedom fight­ers chased prin­ci­ple be­cause power was not on offer, Amit Varma said. “If Nehru was alive today, I posit that he would be Pratap Bhanu Mehta.” {033-C04}

brief.head: Less money, more good
brief.text: Indian econ­o­mists gen­er­ally favour big­ger gov­ern­ment, Ajay Shah said. Yet scep­tics of state spend­ing might con­clude that “the Indian state would do more good if it had less money”. {033-C06}

brief.head: When in doubt, ban it
brief.text: Indian of­fi­cials ban what is hard to un­der­stand or risky, Ajay Shah said: doing good goes un­re­warded, while get­ting into trou­ble “will de­stroy your ca­reer”. {033-C15}

brief.head: The booth knows
brief.text: Results are vis­i­ble booth by booth, about 2,000 peo­ple each, Ajay Shah said, so a win­ning party can re­ward or pun­ish a whole basti. {033-C21}

thought.label: Thought for the day
thought.text: Governments con­sist of peo­ple, right? And peo­ple re­spond to in­cen­tives.
thought.who: Amit Varma, stating the core truth of public choice theory, which he felt should not need saying

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah apply economics to the state
lead.head: The state, minus the halo

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 33

body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah opened the episode bench press­ing. “Put ef­fort. Put ef­fort,” Varma urged. The heav­ier lift­ing was in­tel­lec­tual: why the state so often fails the peo­ple it is meant to serve.

Their tool was pub­lic choice the­ory, which Varma called his favourite branch of eco­nom­ics. It ap­plies the study of how peo­ple re­spond to in­cen­tives to politi­cians, bu­reau­crats, vot­ers and the state.

Its core truth, he said, should not need say­ing: gov­ern­ment is “not some myth­i­cal benev­o­lent beast sit­ting up there”. Governments con­sist of peo­ple, and peo­ple re­spond to in­cen­tives. {033-C01}

There is no sin­gle pub­lic in­ter­est, Varma ar­gued, only dif­fer­ent peo­ple want­ing dif­fer­ent things. That mat­ters in a coun­try whose big­gest re­li­gion, he said, is the re­li­gion of gov­ern­ment.
Shah framed the episode as the third pil­lar of a se­ries on the state, after episodes on what a state is and what it should do.
## Follow the in­cen­tives
Politicians want, above all, to get elected, Varma said. “This au­to­mat­i­cally means that a politician’s time hori­zon is al­ways a short term. It is the next elec­tion.” {033-C03}
So they cater to pop­u­lar sen­ti­ment, and ne­glect poli­cies whose pay­off is long-term or rests on coun­ter­in­tu­itive truths, such as the idea that life is pos­i­tive-sum.

Special in­ter­ests sup­ply the money politi­cians need, and ex­pect a re­turn. The pub­lic sel­dom no­tices, be­cause each per­son loses a rupee while a few gain enor­mously: con­cen­trated ben­e­fits, dif­fuse costs.
Shah added a twist. “The one thing worse than a world where pri­vate firms can lobby with the gov­ern­ment and in­flu­ence pol­icy is one in which they can­not,” he said.

Bureaucrats, Varma said, are mostly good peo­ple, his own fa­ther among them. But they pro­tect and ex­pand their turf. “You are on a gravy train, you want that gravy train to con­tinue as long as pos­si­ble.” {033-C12}
Shah warned that India is be­com­ing an ad­min­is­tra­tive state, where of­fi­cials rule and cit­i­zens are sub­jects.
## Ballots and blind spots
Voters fare no bet­ter. One vote al­most never de­cides an elec­tion, so it is ra­tio­nal not to study man­i­festos, Varma said, cit­ing Anthony Downs’s idea of ra­tio­nal ig­no­rance. {033-C16}
“Voting doesn’t af­fect me in the ev­ery­day,” he said. Shah went fur­ther: he has never voted, be­cause the cost-benefit anal­y­sis never made sense to him.

Varma also weighed first-past-the-post, under which, he said, a party with 35 per cent of the votes can win 80 per cent of the seats, against pro­por­tional rep­re­sen­ta­tion, with­out pick­ing a side.
## The rule­book
The in­cen­tives, Varma said, come from how the state is de­signed, and the con­sti­tu­tion writes the rules of the game.
His test of a good sys­tem is whether the worst per­son in the world could come to power and still do lit­tle dam­age, be­cause the state sim­ply lacks the power. {033-C22}
India’s Constitution, he ar­gued, pro­tects the state more than the cit­i­zen. Shah said he was not that un­happy with the state of af­fairs, plac­ing his hopes in the basic struc­ture doc­trine.
Shah signed off call­ing pub­lic choice dis­con­cert­ing, but “the cold re­al­ity of the world that we should think of the state as an op­ti­miz­ing bunch of peo­ple”.

second.label: The public purse
second.head: Other people’s money
second.deck: Amit Varma borrows Milton Friedman’s matrix to show how governments spend

pic.caption: Milton Friedman in New York in 1986

body: Amit Varma reached for a ma­trix drawn up by the econ­o­mist Milton Friedman. Spend your own money on your­self, and you economise and seek value. Spend it on a stranger, and you economise but hardly care about value.

Spend some­one else’s money on your­self, and you seek value but do not economise. Spend some­body else’s money on some­body else, and you do nei­ther. “This is the whole busi­ness of gov­ern­ment,” Varma said. {033-C05}

Ajay Shah added PJ O’Rourke’s line that giv­ing money and power to politi­cians is like giv­ing whiskey and car keys to teenagers. {033-J05} Varma raised him HL Mencken: every elec­tion is “a sort of an ad­vanced auc­tion sale of stolen goods”.

quote.text: And if I spend some­body else’s money on some­body else, I will nei­ther econ­o­mize nor seek value.

third.head: A bad bet on online poker

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Sheldon Adelson and online poker

body: Sheldon Adelson owned phys­i­cal casi­nos, among them the Sands and the Venetian. For many years, Amit Varma said, he lob­bied to keep on­line poker banned, and he was one of the big fun­ders of the Republican Party.
Varma, who has been a pro­fes­sional poker player, watched from the in­side. Adelson, he said, was much hated among poker pro­fes­sion­als. He be­lieved on­line poker threat­ened his casi­nos.
“Actually, it is kinda ironic that it re­ally wasn’t,” Varma said. “It’s just that the ecosys­tem of gam­bling ex­panded when on­line poker came in. It didn’t hurt the live casi­nos.” {033-S02}

Such cap­ture by spe­cial in­ter­ests is far worse in the US than in India, Varma said, rec­om­mend­ing Jonathan Rauch’s *Government’s End* as “a scary read”. India is not there yet, he said, but could eas­ily get there. {033-R06}

box.title: The gateway drug
box.text: Many date the field, Amit Varma said, to James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock’s *The Calculus of Consent* in 1962. His own way in, his “gate­way drug”, was Eamonn Butler’s *Public Choice: A Primer*, mas­ter­ful and read­able in under an hour. {033-R01}

sections.label: The premise
sections.head: No benevolent beast
sections.caption: governments as people
body: Public choice the­ory, Amit Varma said, is his favourite branch of eco­nom­ics. It takes the study of how peo­ple re­spond to in­cen­tives under scarcity and ap­plies it to pol­i­tics: politi­cians, bu­reau­cracy, elec­tions, vot­ing and the state.

Its core truth seems ob­vi­ous, he said, but needs say­ing any­way. Government is not a benev­o­lent being; gov­ern­ments con­sist of peo­ple, who are “frail”, “flawed” and “often ra­tio­nal”. {033-C01}
Nor is there a pub­lic in­ter­est for them to serve, he said: dif­fer­ent peo­ple want dif­fer­ent things. “There is no ag­gre­gated thing.”
## A com­mu­nity with guns

Ajay Shah brought in Max Weber. The state, in Weber’s def­i­ni­tion, is not a col­lec­tion of in­sti­tu­tions but “a com­mu­nity of peo­ple that achieve and main­tain the mo­nop­oly of phys­i­cal vi­o­lence on a ter­ri­tory”. {033-C02}

Rule-bound, pre­dictable in­sti­tu­tions are an as­pi­ra­tion, Shah said, and every gov­ern­ment achieves them to a dif­fer­ent de­gree. So the econ­o­mist should ask what the peo­ple in­side the state are max­imis­ing, and pre­dict how they will wield its co­er­cive power.
Varma added a cau­tion. Even “com­mu­nity” is too col­lec­tive: a com­mu­nity does not have val­ues, only the peo­ple within it do.
~ This mat­ters most in India, he ar­gued, where the big­gest re­li­gion is the re­li­gion of gov­ern­ment, and *Mai Baap Sarkar* is ex­pected to solve every prob­lem. {033-J15}

quote.text: There is no such thing as a pub­lic in­ter­est.

sections.label: Politicians
sections.head: Thinking only till polling day
sections.caption: the politician’s short horizon
body: The num­ber one in­cen­tive of a politi­cian, Amit Varma said, is to get elected. So the time hori­zon is al­ways the next elec­tion, and a party leader al­ways faces a local elec­tion some­where. {033-C03}

Good poli­cies often rest on coun­ter­in­tu­itive in­sights: that life is pos­i­tive-sum, not zero-sum, and that mar­kets, lan­guages and nat­u­ral se­lec­tion work by bot­tom-up evo­lu­tion. People are con­di­tioned in­stead to want a strong leader who, if prices are too high, says: “I will fix the price.”
He also re­called a fa­mous car­toon: two wolves and a sheep, vot­ing on what to have for din­ner.
## Spending with­out care
Politicians con­trol enor­mous sums, and by Milton Friedman’s ma­trix, Varma said, those who spend some­body else’s money on some­body else nei­ther economise nor seek value. {033-C05}

Varma claims to have writ­ten the first pub­lic choice lim­er­ick, for his weekly slot in the *Times of India*: “A neta who loves cur­rency notes / told me what his line of work de­notes. / It is kind of funny, / we steal people’s money / and use some of it to buy their votes.” {033-J01}

~ Asked by Ajay Shah whether this was be­fore ChatGPT, Varma said ChatGPT can­not write lim­er­icks “be­cause it can’t count”: a good lim­er­ick needs nine, nine, six, six and nine syl­la­bles. {033-J02}

quote.text: We steal people’s money and use some of it to buy their votes.

sections.label: Special interests
sections.head: Your rupee, their windfall
sections.caption: concentrated benefits and diffuse costs
body: Politicians need tons of money, Amit Varma said, and spe­cial in­ter­ests sup­ply it as an in­vest­ment that will need a re­turn, usu­ally through poli­cies that shield them from com­pe­ti­tion or re­dis­tribute wealth to them.

The pub­lic does not no­tice be­cause of a phe­nom­e­non Varma cred­ited to Mancur Olson: con­cen­trated ben­e­fits and dif­fuse costs. If the gov­ern­ment took one rupee from ev­ery­one and gave it to Ajay Shah, “ev­ery­body who’s los­ing one rupee, they don’t even know they’re los­ing one rupee”. {033-C08}
Shah, mean­while, would be get­ting “one point seven bil­lion ru­pees or what­ever it is”, and would gladly give his local politi­cian ten per cent. {#billion}
Small traders, vot­ers and fun­ders for some par­ties, can keep FDI out of re­tail, and con­sumers pay more for less with­out notic­ing.
## Worse than lob­by­ing

Shah com­pli­cated the pic­ture. In London, New York or Tokyo, he said, firms openly lobby and dis­agree with of­fi­cials, which dis­perses power. In India, reg­u­la­tors hold ar­bi­trary power and in­dus­try has been co­erced into si­lence. “The one thing worse than a world where pri­vate firms can lobby with the gov­ern­ment and in­flu­ence pol­icy is one in which they can­not.” {033-C11}
~ Varma agreed, but put the deeper prob­lem else­where: in an ideal world, the state would not have the power to block entry into a mar­ket at all.

quote.text: Which is why I say all in­ter­ven­tions in free mar­kets are re­dis­tri­bu­tions from the poor to the rich.

sections.label: Bureaucrats
sections.head: All aboard the gravy train
sections.caption: bureaucrats and their turf
body: Amit Varma’s fa­ther was an IAS of­fi­cer, “a good man”, and “per­haps a lit­tle too hon­est, or com­pletely hon­est”. So Varma re­jects the stereo­type of the cor­rupt babu: most bu­reau­crats are good peo­ple re­spond­ing to in­cen­tives. {033-S07}

He found those in­cen­tives in *Parkinson’s Law*, by C Northcote Parkinson, a clas­sic of com­edy that is also a pub­lic choice book. Work ex­pands to fill the time avail­able; of­fi­cials mul­ti­ply sub­or­di­nates, not ri­vals, and grow their bud­gets and turf. {033-R07}
The re­sult is re­sis­tance to change and a sta­tus quo bias. Someone who would agree from out­side that a min­istry should be abol­ished, Varma said, will de­fend it once in­side.
## Not just suit­cases

Ajay Shah de­scribed an ad­min­is­tra­tive state, in which the leg­is­la­ture and the ju­di­ciary stop act­ing as checks and of­fi­cials rule over sub­jects. That, he said, is the prob­lem India faces today. {033-C13}

He blamed Bollywood for re­duc­ing cor­rup­tion to suit­cases of cash. His own def­i­ni­tion: doing things not aligned with the organisation’s pro­fes­sional ob­jec­tives for per­sonal gain. {033-C14} That cov­ers favours to friends and fam­ily, ca­reer-boosting ex­pe­di­ency and lazi­ness: “You get the power of a civil ser­vant and you do no work.”
~ His rem­edy is more democ­racy, he said: real checks and bal­ances, and many sources of power out­side gov­ern­ment, so that of­fi­cials feel the burn when things go wrong.

quote.text: The ad­min­is­tra­tive state is one in which power gets con­cen­trated into the of­fi­cials.

sections.label: Voters
sections.head: The rationally ignorant voter
sections.caption: rational ignorance
body: Ajay Shah called elec­tions “the great tem­ple of the Amar Chitra Katha ver­sion of democ­racy”. Amit Varma began in­stead with Bollywood: the film *Newton*, in which Rajkummar Rao’s elec­tion of­fi­cer finds that the peo­ple who turn up do not care who is on the bal­lot. {033-S04}
That, Varma said, is Anthony Downs’s ra­tio­nal ig­no­rance. One vote al­most never de­cides an elec­tion, so it is ra­tio­nal to spend scarce time and at­ten­tion else­where. {033-C16}

A lis­tener once cor­rected him: a local elec­tion in India had been de­cided by one vote, and the loser’s wife had not gone to vote. His ad­vice: “kindly if your spouse is in an elec­tion, kindly vote.” {033-S05}
## Votes for sale
Tactical vot­ing hides people’s true pref­er­ences, Varma said, cit­ing Kenneth Arrow’s im­pos­si­bil­ity the­o­rem: a po­lit­i­cal mar­ket­place can­not sat­isfy them.

Shah added that Vitalik Buterin had told them it is too easy to bribe peo­ple to vote against their in­ter­est. In India, Shah said, pol­i­tics goes one basti at a time, and “the high­est bid­der gets those votes”. {033-S09}
~ Why vote at all? Out of a norm, Varma said, like sig­nalling a left turn on an empty road, “un­less you’re in Bombay and you drive like me”. {033-J10}

quote.text: You vote for the same rea­son that you go to a Manchester United game.

portraits.caption: Kenneth Arrow
portraits.credit: Linda A. Cicero / Stanford News Service, CC BY 3.0

sections.label: The constitution
sections.head: A state too weak to harm
sections.caption: the rules of the game
body: Public choice, Amit Varma said, teaches the most im­por­tant thing of all: the rules of the game. Incentives come from the de­sign of the state, and the con­sti­tu­tion sets that de­sign.

A good con­sti­tu­tion pro­tects peo­ple from the state. India’s, writ­ten when it was un­clear whether the princely states would join, cen­tralised power and copied the colo­nial state, he said. Free speech gets lip ser­vice, hedged by caveats such as pub­lic order and de­cency. {033-C23}

Every gov­ern­ment from Nehru on­wards, he said, amended the Constitution when­ever it wanted to do some­thing un­con­sti­tu­tional. He re­called a car­toon in which the Parliament book­shop stocks only books, “not pe­ri­od­i­cals”. {033-J12}
## The elite’s doc­u­ment

Ajay Shah doubted that suc­cess­ful con­sti­tu­tions re­flect the con­sen­sus Buchanan and Tullock wanted. Most are elite projects, he said; the German and Japanese ones were partly im­posed. Varma in­ter­jected: “Elite rather than elit­ist.”

India, Shah said, “lucked out and got a fairly bad doc­u­ment”. {033-J13} Its real con­sti­tu­tion is the basic struc­ture, which the ju­di­ciary has mostly de­fended, while the rest is amended like any other law. {033-C24}
~ That pushes India, he ar­gued, to­wards some­thing like the British un­writ­ten tra­di­tion, where the work lies in ap­ply­ing the basic struc­ture doc­trine wisely.

quote.text: So you have a rel­a­tively lib­eral con­sti­tu­tion im­posed on an il­lib­eral so­ci­ety by a bunch of un­elected peo­ple.
The best sys­tem that I can think of is a sys­tem in which the worst per­son in the world, and Adolf Hitler even, can get to power and not man­age to do any dam­age

p3.title: Tales of the state
p3.deck: Bootleggers, bribes, an unbought shirt and a reform that nearly happened

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s quiz: Shah Rukh Khan and public choice theory
stories.head: Raees picks the wrong fight
body: Amit Varma had a quiz ques­tion for Ajay Shah: what does Shah Rukh Khan’s film *Raees* have to do with pub­lic choice the­ory? Shah did not know, and had not seen the film. “Good,” said Varma. {033-S03}

In the film, Shah Rukh Khan plays a macho boot­leg­ger in Gujarat, where al­co­hol is banned. One day a politi­cian sets out on a *Darubandi Yatra*, a rally de­mand­ing that al­co­hol be banned, and the boot­leg­ger wants to stop him.
This, Varma said, makes no ra­tio­nal sense, “be­cause ac­tu­ally the boot­leg­ger and the politi­cian who wants al­co­hol banned, their in­ter­ests are the same, they’re on the same side.”

There is a phrase for it, boot­leg­gers and Baptists, coined by the reg­u­la­tory econ­o­mist Bruce Yandle. The Baptist says al­co­hol is evil, that it breaks fam­i­lies apart, and must be banned. “So the Baptist gets al­co­hol banned,” Varma said. “So al­co­hol is banned, and then the boot­leg­ger comes in.” {033-C10}
The boot­leg­ger sup­plies the banned *daru*. The two work for the same ends, Varma said, and some­times they are lit­er­ally hand in hand.
So in his ver­sion, the Shah Rukh char­ac­ter would back the politi­cian in­stead: “*Yatra karo*, I will dance at your wed­ding also.” {033-J04}

~ The same logic hides be­hind many pious-sounding rules, Varma said. We think a ban on FDI in re­tail pro­tects small traders, while “your money is being taken away and given to those guys”. The an­swer is to dig: “You got to ask why is this hap­pen­ing.”
stories.why: Moral cru­saders and those who profit from a ban can look like en­e­mies and still be quiet al­lies. Before trust­ing a reg­u­la­tion that sounds pious, ask who gains from it, and how.
stories.postscript: Varma once ran a col­umn, *Housefull Economics*, ex­plain­ing eco­nom­ics through films, and asked view­ers whether they would like a reg­u­lar seg­ment on the show.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Shah Rukh Khan’s bootlegger

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on rent-seeking, one restaurant at a time
stories.head: Too many doors, too few doors
body: A friend of Amit Varma’s owned a restau­rant in Bangalore. The fire de­part­ment told him he needed mul­ti­ple en­trances. The ex­cise de­part­ment told him he could have only one, so that it could track al­co­hol going in and out. {033-S01}
“And all of them are tak­ing bribes from the poor guy,” Varma said, “no mat­ter how many doors he has.”

This, Varma said, is rent-seeking, a term that has noth­ing to do with rent­ing out prop­erty. When the state con­trols some­thing or cre­ates an ar­ti­fi­cial scarcity, it can make a lot of money off it. {033-C07}
~ His hy­po­thet­i­cal was closer to home: a gov­ern­ment that de­cides pod­cast­ers need a li­cence, re­new­able every six months. “And of course I have to pay a bribe for it.” {033-J03}
stories.why: When the state con­trols per­mis­sions and its rules con­tra­dict each other, no one can com­ply, what­ever they do. That im­pos­si­bil­ity is ex­actly what of­fi­cials can charge for. Varma ex­plored restau­rant reg­u­la­tion fur­ther in an episode of *The Seen and the Unseen* with Madhu Menon.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the restaurant’s doors

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the electoral reform India nearly adopted
stories.head: The reform that almost got through
body: Jayaprakash Narayan, Amit Varma re­called from an old episode of *The Seen and the Unseen*, al­most got India to adopt pro­por­tional rep­re­sen­ta­tion. He had friends in high places, and when the UPA was in charge all the prin­ci­pal play­ers had agreed. {033-R18}
Then Sonia Gandhi said no. Her sense, Varma said, was that Congress would be in power for­ever under first-past-the-post, and the change would hurt it.

“Now the irony of that,” Varma said, “is that had pro­por­tional rep­re­sen­ta­tion got through the BJP would not be so dom­i­nant today and the Congress would have many more seats than they do.” {033-S06}

~ Varma did not take a side. Pratap Bhanu Mehta, he said, told him it would be an ab­so­lute dis­as­ter that would tear the coun­try apart. Varma counts both men among the country’s tallest in­tel­lec­tu­als.
stories.why: Those who block a re­form be­cause they think their power is per­ma­nent can end up harmed by that choice. And elec­toral de­sign is gen­uinely con­tested, even among the wis­est peo­ple. {033-C19}
stories.postscript: Ajay Shah noted that post-war Germany, de­sign­ing against an­other Hitler, chose pro­por­tional rep­re­sen­ta­tion after much de­bate. {033-S08}

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on not voting as a signal
stories.head: Nothing on the rack worth buying
body: Amit Varma once skipped an elec­tion. No party seemed worth vot­ing for, and he did not want to vote tac­ti­cally for the least evil. Someone told him that, not hav­ing voted, he should have no opin­ion on the re­sult.

He dis­agreed strongly. If every shirt in a mall is bad, he said, you need not buy one. “My not buy­ing a shirt is a sig­nal that there is a gap in the mar­ket and maybe that can be ful­filled.” {033-S10}
The many Indians who do not vote, he ar­gued, sig­nal to po­lit­i­cal en­trepreneurs that ex­ist­ing par­ties are not meet­ing de­mand.

~ That, he said, is ex­actly what the Aam Aadmi Party did. Varma does not like AAP, but calls it a re­mark­ably suc­cess­ful ex­er­cise in po­lit­i­cal en­trepreneur­ship: it of­fered dis­af­fected mid­dle-class vot­ers some­one like them, talk­ing about cor­rup­tion.
stories.why: Staying away from the polls is in­for­ma­tion too. Gaps in the po­lit­i­cal mar­ket get filled by new en­trants, for bet­ter or worse: cor­rup­tion, Varma noted, is the first ral­ly­ing cry of pop­ulist move­ments.
stories.postscript: Ajay Shah has never voted: the cost-benefit anal­y­sis, he said, never made sense to him. {033-J11}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the shirt nobody bought

overheard.text: I re­ally think of the elec­tions as a bat­tle to be the one legal mafia for five years.
overheard.who: Amit Varma, on what Indian elections really decide

quiz.q: What does the Shah Rukh Khan film *Raees* get wrong about public choice, according to Varma?
quiz.a: Its boot­leg­ger fights a pro­hi­bi­tion­ist who is re­ally on his side.

quiz.q: Why did a Bangalore restaurant owner pay bribes whatever number of doors he had?
quiz.a: The fire de­part­ment wanted many en­trances, ex­cise only one, and all took bribes.

quiz.q: In Milton Friedman’s matrix, what happens when you spend somebody else’s money on somebody else?
quiz.a: You nei­ther economise nor seek value: the whole busi­ness of gov­ern­ment, Varma said.

quiz.q: Which regulatory economist coined the phrase ‘bootleggers and Baptists’, according to Amit Varma?
quiz.a: Bruce Yandle, whose phrase pairs the moral­ist with the man who prof­its.

quiz.q: Why, by Anthony Downs’s idea of rational ignorance, do voters not study party manifestos?
quiz.a: One vote al­most never de­cides an elec­tion, so at­ten­tion is bet­ter spent else­where.

quiz.q: Why has Ajay Shah never voted in an election, by his own account?
quiz.a: He never felt the cost-benefit anal­y­sis made sense; why peo­ple vote mys­ti­fies him.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 33. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Max Weber (Ernst Gottmann, public domain); James M. Buchanan (Atlas Network Official website, CC BY-SA 3.0); Milton Friedman (Bachrach Studios, public domain); Kenneth Arrow (Linda A. Cicero / Stanford News Service, CC BY 3.0); Jawaharlal Nehru (Keystone View Company/FPG, public domain); Gordon Tullock (Joshua Paquin, CC BY 2.5); Jonathan Rauch (New America, CC BY 2.0).

shelf.title: Public Choice – A Primer
shelf.creator: Eamonn Butler
shelf.why: A short, mas­ter­ful in­tro­duc­tion to pub­lic choice the­ory, read­able in under an hour, that ex­plains why state fail­ure is prac­ti­cally ev­ery­where though ev­ery­one talks only of mar­ket fail­ure.

shelf.title: The Calculus of Consent
shelf.creator: James M Buchanan and Gordon Tullock
shelf.why: The found­ing text of pub­lic choice the­ory, which frames a con­sti­tu­tion as the ‘rules of the game’ that should ide­ally rest on con­sen­sus.

shelf.title: The Logic of Collective Action
shelf.creator: Mancur Olson
shelf.why: Olson’s ac­count of ‘con­cen­trated ben­e­fits and dif­fuse costs’: why small, or­gan­ised in­ter­est groups beat the large, un­or­gan­ised pub­lic.

shelf.title: An Economic Theory of Democracy
shelf.creator: Anthony Downs
shelf.why: Amit first learned about ra­tio­nal ig­no­rance from this book: the idea that vot­ers sen­si­bly don’t spend scarce at­ten­tion on a vote that al­most never de­cides any­thing.

shelf.title: Books by William A Niskanen
shelf.creator: William A Niskanen
shelf.why: Amit says Niskanen has great books on the in­cen­tives of bu­reau­crats.

shelf.title: Government’s End: Why Washington Stopped Working
shelf.creator: Jonathan Rauch
shelf.why: Rauch’s ac­count of how spe­cial in­ter­ests cap­tured the American state, coin­ing ‘demosclerosis’: in­ter­est groups and reg­u­la­tions mul­ti­ply until they are nearly im­pos­si­ble to re­verse and crowd out other pol­i­cy­mak­ing.

shelf.title: Parkinson’s Law
shelf.creator: C Northcote Parkinson
shelf.why: Amit calls it a clas­sic book of com­edy that is also a pub­lic choice book.

shelf.title: Shruti Rajagopalan on our constitutional amendments
shelf.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
shelf.why: Shruti Rajagopalan’s talk trac­ing how India’s Constitution has been amended from Nehru on­wards when­ever gov­ern­ments wanted to do some­thing un­con­sti­tu­tional, until amend­ment be­came the rou­tine way to make the un­con­sti­tu­tional con­sti­tu­tional.

shelf.title: Where Have All the Leaders Gone?
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s pub­lic-choice an­swer to why the free­dom strug­gle at­tracted peo­ple of prin­ci­ple while today’s cen­tralised state at­tracts ca­reerists chas­ing power and money.

shelf.title: The Great Redistribution
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s ar­gu­ment that mar­ket in­ter­ven­tions such as tar­iffs or bans on FDI in re­tail qui­etly move money from many dis­persed, poor con­sumers to a few or­gan­ised, rich in­ter­est groups, the op­po­site of their stated in­ten­tion.

shelf.title: Price Controls Lead to Shortages and Harm the Poor
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s case that you can­not leg­is­late scarcity away: price caps dis­cour­age pro­duc­ers and in­no­va­tors, so goods don’t get cheaper but van­ish into short­ages and black mar­kets, hurt­ing the poor they claim to pro­tect.

shelf.title: Politics (limerick)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It cap­tures the link be­tween money and power in five lines.

shelf.title: A Few Thoughts on Limericks
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: For read­ers who want to un­der­stand the craft, in­clud­ing the ideal 9-9-6-6-9 syl­la­ble count.

shelf.title: Housefull Economics on Pragati
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It ex­plains eco­nomic con­cepts through films.

shelf.title: The Economics of Voting
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Further read­ing on the vot­ing ques­tions dis­cussed in the episode, such as ra­tio­nal ig­no­rance and why peo­ple vote at all.

shelf.title: Restaurant Regulations — Episode 18 of The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Madhu Menon
shelf.why: Madhu Menon on how restau­rant reg­u­la­tion in India works as an op­por­tu­nity for rent-seeking: an over­reach­ing state makes hon­est busi­ness im­pos­si­ble and bribes un­avoid­able.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of KP Krishnan — Episode 355 of The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with KP Krishnan
shelf.why: An eight-hour oral his­tory from a re­former in­side the Indian state: how India han­dled the 2008 cri­sis, fought for in­fla­tion tar­get­ing and built the bank­ruptcy code.

shelf.title: A Life in Indian Politics — Episode 149 of The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Jayaprakash Narayan
shelf.why: Jayaprakash Narayan tells how India al­most adopted pro­por­tional rep­re­sen­ta­tion, until Sonia Gandhi said no.

shelf.title: The Gentle Wisdom of Pratap Bhanu Mehta — Episode 300 of The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Pratap Bhanu Mehta
shelf.why: It gives the op­pos­ing view to JP’s: Pratap Bhanu Mehta be­lieves PR would be an ab­so­lute dis­as­ter for India.

shelf.title: The Anti-Defection Law — Episode 13 of The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Barun Mitra
shelf.why: Barun Mitra on how a well-meant law to stop horse-trading turned MPs into votes that fol­low the whip, one of the things Amit sees get­ting in the way of Indian democ­racy.

shelf.title: Our Parliament and Our Democracy — Episode 253 of The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with MR Madhavan
shelf.why: A long con­ver­sa­tion with MR Madhavan on how India’s par­lia­men­tary rules, es­pe­cially the anti-defection law, weaken its democ­racy.

shelf.title: Vitalik Buterin Fights the Dragon-Tyrant — Episode 342 of The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah with Vitalik Buterin
shelf.why: A three-way con­ver­sa­tion with Vitalik Buterin on pol­i­tics and iden­tity, the source of his in­sight that the core weak­ness of vot­ing sys­tems is how eas­ily peo­ple can be bribed, and of Ajay’s ar­gu­ment that cash’s anonymity pro­tects us from a sur­veil­lance so­ci­ety.

shelf.title: The First Assault on Our Constitution — Episode 194 of The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Tripurdaman Singh
shelf.why: Tripurdaman Singh on the First Amendment to India’s Constitution, which Amit says badly harmed free speech in India: a con­ver­sa­tional way into the story Singh tells in Sixteen Stormy Days.

shelf.title: Public Choice Theory — Episode 121 of The Seen and the Unseen
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A com­pan­ion for lis­ten­ers who want more on pub­lic choice the­ory.

shelf.title: Understanding the State — Episode 25 of Everything is Everything
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The foun­da­tion of the show’s think­ing on gov­ern­ment: the state is a mo­nop­oly on vi­o­lence that acts through co­er­cion, so every in­ter­ven­tion, paid for by taxes, must be jus­ti­fied.

shelf.title: When Should the State Act? — Episode 26 of Everything is Everything
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on mar­ket fail­ure in its pre­cise tech­ni­cal sense (pub­lic goods, ex­ter­nal­i­ties and the rest) and on the nar­row con­di­tions under which the state may in­ter­vene, con­di­tions that are nec­es­sary but not suf­fi­cient.

laughs.text: Amit claims to have writ­ten the first pub­lic choice lim­er­ick ever, for his weekly Times of India slot: ‘A neta who loves cur­rency notes / told me what his line of work de­notes. / It is kind of funny, / we steal people’s money / and use some of it to buy their votes.’
Ajay: ‘This is even be­fore ChatGPT?’ Amit: ChatGPT ‘can’t write lim­er­icks be­cause it can’t count, it can’t do math’, and a good lim­er­ick needs a 9-9-6-6-9 syl­la­ble count, not just rhymes.

Amit’s rent-seeking hy­po­thet­i­cal: the gov­ern­ment de­cides peo­ple like Amit Varma and Ajay Shah can’t pod­cast with­out a li­cence, ‘re­new­able every six months. And of course I have to pay a bribe for it.’

Amit sets Ajay a quiz on what Raees has to do with pub­lic choice the­ory. Ajay doesn’t know and hasn’t seen the film. Amit: ‘Good.’ His ver­dict on the plot: SRK’s boot­leg­ger should be back­ing the pro­hi­bi­tion­ist politi­cian: ‘Yatra karo, I will dance at your wed­ding also.’
Ajay on why Indians think cor­rup­tion means suit­cases of cash: ‘I blame Bollywood for this.’

Listing the many voices that should mat­ter in a lib­eral democ­racy (jour­nal­ists, in­tel­lec­tu­als, busi­nesses, NGOs), Ajay adds: ‘Podcasters should mat­ter. Podcasters should mat­ter above all.’

Ajay calls elec­tions ‘the great tem­ple of the Amar Chitra Katha ver­sion of democracy’, where the peo­ple vote and all prob­lems are solved. Amit replies that first he wants to talk about ‘the great tem­ple of Indian en­ter­tain­ment, which is Bollywood.’
Amit says peo­ple sig­nal left turns even on an empty road be­cause it is a habit, ‘un­less you’re in Bombay and you drive like me.’
Ajay’s con­fes­sion: ‘I am very sad to say, but I have not voted be­cause I never felt the cost ben­e­fit anal­y­sis made sense and it has been a mys­tery to me why peo­ple vote.’
Amit re­calls an old car­toon: some­one asks the Parliament book­shop for the Constitution and is told, ‘we only stock books here, not pe­ri­od­i­cals.’

Ajay on India’s con­sti­tu­tional mo­ment: ‘some peo­ple wrote a United States Constitution, some peo­ple wrote the Constitution of India, and we lucked out and got a fairly bad doc­u­ment.’ Earlier, Amit cor­rected him mid-sentence: ‘Elite rather than elit­ist.’

Quote duel: Ajay cites PJ O’Rourke (‘giv­ing money and power to politi­cians is like giv­ing whiskey and car keys to teenagers’). Amit replies: ‘You throw a PJ O’Rourke quote at me, I will raise you with HL Mencken’: every elec­tion is ‘a sort of an ad­vanced auc­tion sale of stolen goods.’
Ajay: ‘There’s no Mahalanobis and Nehru any­more. Nobody is dream­ing what the coun­try wants to be.’ Amit: ‘And in a sense, thank God that’s gone.’
Mai Baap Sarkar: Amit’s name for India’s ‘re­li­gion of government’, the be­lief that a parental state should solve every prob­lem.
The two wolves and a sheep car­toon: ma­jor­ity vot­ing on what to have for din­ner, used as Amit’s image of the dan­gers of democ­racy.
Kenneth Arrow’s im­pos­si­bil­ity the­o­rem, which Amit cites to argue that a po­lit­i­cal mar­ket­place can’t sat­isfy people’s true pref­er­ences.
